how-much-to-charge-for-hydro-jetting.htm.text:
← Hydro-jet and sewer camera bid calculator

How much to charge for hydro-jetting

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$149 drain special,” or a price they saw for hydro-jetting on a coupon site. That number is not a takeoff. A 50-foot kitchen cable from an existing cleanout is not the same job as a 140-foot main with a toilet pull, roots at the street, 150 feet of hose from the truck, and a camera warranty pass. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the extra footage and the access, not just the trip

Septic-pumping calculators price a tank lid, a hose, and extra gallons. Water-heater calculators price a vent, a gas upsize, and an attic. Kitchen-hood calculators price a canopy and a rooftop fan. Dryer-vent calculators price a lint run and a roof cap. A hydro-jet or sewer camera job is a line: the machine, the footage past the included run, how you get into the pipe, and the camera that proves the work. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first toilet pull eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra foot past the included run is time that never appears on the coupon. A toilet pull is billed as its own hours and a wax ring. Roots, grease, a second line, and hose distance from the truck are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 140-foot main jet-plus-camera with a toilet pull, roots, and 150 feet of hose prices about $987 ($7 per foot of line, 7.1 crew-hours). The same shop’s 50-foot kitchen cable from a cleanout prices about $309 ($6 per foot, 2.0 hours, walk-away $201). Matching the brochure job’s $149 special on the toilet-pull main is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the special itself is already $201.

A commercial kitchen jet is not automatically the expensive one

An 80-foot commercial kitchen jet with grease, a second line, and a new cleanout is not the 140-foot toilet-pull main plus 100%. On the sample rates that kitchen job prices about $960 ($12 per foot, 6.9 crew-hours) — similar money to the long main, not because the jet is cheaper but because the new cleanout and the second line do not live in a published special. A 75-foot main jet-plus-camera from a cleanout with light grease prices about $632 (4.3 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first wax ring.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h tech loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a plumbing specification, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Line footage, access, roots, grease, disposal, and whether a camera pass is required are yours to confirm.

Price your hydro-jet or camera job

Common questions

How much to charge for hydro-jetting?

Charge from the trip, the machine (camera, cable, or hydro-jet), extra footage past the included run, access (cleanout versus toilet pull versus a new cleanout), roots, grease, hose distance from the truck, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 50-foot kitchen cable from a cleanout at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $309 — about $6 per foot of line.

Why is a $149 drain special dangerous?

Homeowners count the trip. Extra footage, a toilet pull, roots, grease, hose distance, and a camera warranty pass do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a 50-foot cleanout cable is how a 140-foot main becomes a two-hour loss.

How much to charge for a sewer camera inspection?

A camera-only pass is not a hydro-jet. On the sample rates a 75-foot main jet-plus-camera from a cleanout with light grease prices around $632 ($8 per foot, 4.3 crew-hours), while a 50-foot kitchen cable special prices around $309 ($6 per foot, 2.0 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not plumbing, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

      Common questions

      Why does a toilet pull or new cleanout cost more than an existing cleanout job?

Match the access option to what's actually on site rather than assuming every job starts the same way.

      Why does a “$149 drain special” price so much lower than this tool's number?

      A flat brochure price usually covers a short run from an existing cleanout with no roots, no grease, and no camera pass — extra footage past the included run, roots, grease, hose distance from the truck, and a camera warranty pass all add hours the flat price never counted. Enter your actual line feet and conditions to see what the special would need to charge to still be profitable.

      Does the camera pass replace a real sewer inspection or a home-sale scope report?

      No. This prices your labor and equipment time for running a camera, not a certified inspection report, a real-estate condition disclosure, or a code determination about the line's condition. Whatever the camera finds is still something you (or a licensed inspector) has to interpret and document separately.

      Is the footage-included assumption accurate for my trucks?

      The included footage and hose-run figures are common ballpark starting points, not a manufacturer spec for your specific jet unit or cable machine. Replace them with what your actual equipment carries so the “extra footage” charge kicks in at the right point.

vs-building-your-own-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Hydro-Jet and Sewer Camera Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. building your own spreadsheet

A spreadsheet can hold the same footage, access, and condition line items this calculator does. Where a hand-built sheet most often drifts from a correct bid is the margin formula, the loaded wage, and keeping three mutually exclusive access methods from double-counting.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can track every input this calculator does — trip hours, line footage past the included run, access method, roots, grease, a second line, hose run from the truck, material costs, loaded wage, overhead, and target margin. None of the arithmetic is exotic on its own. What tends to go wrong is the formula that turns a pile of costs into a price: price = cost * (1 + margin%) computes a markup, not a margin. At a 30% target on $700 of direct cost plus overhead, that mistake prices the job at $910 instead of the $1,000 a true 30% margin requires — a $90 gap that reads as a correct bid right up until you check what share of the price is actually profit.

This calculator uses price = totalCost / (1 - targetMargin / 100), so the margin you type is the margin you get. It also loads the hourly wage by payroll burden before multiplying by hours, keeps toilet-pull, new-cleanout, and roof-vent access mutually exclusive so there's nothing to double-count, and applies overhead to the full direct cost — labor, materials, and travel together — rather than to labor alone.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can a spreadsheet hold the same footage, access, and condition line items?Yes — the fields are the same either way.
Does typing a 30% target margin into the price formula actually return a 30% margin?This calculator — a hand-built cost * (1 + margin%) formula returns a markup, which understates the price for the same target.
Is the payroll burden rate actually wired into the labor cost, or just sitting in its own cell?This calculator loads the wage by burden before multiplying by hours, every time.
Could two access-method cells (toilet pull, new cleanout, roof vent) get filled in and double-count hours?This calculator keeps the three mutually exclusive. A spreadsheet with one column per method can't guarantee that on its own.
Is overhead applied to the whole direct cost, or only to the labor row it happened to be wired to?This calculator applies it to labor, materials, and travel together.
I want a running log of every job I've bid, or a shared file for a bookkeeper.A spreadsheet — this calculator stores nothing and keeps no history.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this calculator?

It can hold the same fields -- trip hours, footage past the included run, access method, roots, grease, hose run, materials, wage, overhead, and target margin. Where a hand-built sheet most often drifts is the formula that turns total cost into a price: writing price = cost * (1 + margin%) computes a markup, not a margin. At a 30% target on $700 of cost, that mistake prices the job at $910 instead of the $1,000 a true 30% margin requires -- a $90 gap that looks like a correct bid until you check what share of the price is actually profit.

What does this calculator get right that a spreadsheet bid sheet often gets wrong?

Three things past the margin formula: it loads the hourly wage by payroll burden before multiplying by hours, so a burden rate typed into its own cell but never wired into the labor formula can't silently understate labor cost. It keeps toilet-pull, new-cleanout, and roof-vent access as mutually exclusive, so there's no risk of a sheet that lets two access-method cells get filled in and double-counts the hours. And it applies overhead to the full direct cost -- labor, materials, and travel together -- rather than to labor alone, which a sheet built one line at a time can miss if overhead was only wired to the labor row.

When is a spreadsheet the better choice?

When you want to keep a running log of every job you've bid, customize the line items for a service this calculator doesn't cover, or share a file with a bookkeeper. This calculator stores nothing and keeps no history -- it exists to get one job's price right on the spot, not to replace your records.

vs-jobber.html.text:
← Hydro-Jet and Sewer Camera Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a plumbing or drain-cleaning business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this sewer camera, cable, or hydro-jet job cost, given its footage and access, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the work type (camera, cable, hydro-jet, or a combo pass), line footage past the included run, access method (existing cleanout, toilet pull, new cleanout, or roof vent), roots, grease, hose run from the truck, and a second line, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, the hour split between the trip, the machine pass, extra footage, and access, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

I need one shared account so my whole crew is scheduling, invoicing, and collecting payment the same way.Jobber, or a comparable field-service platform.

Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Jobber is used through a subscription account.

Most plumbing and drain-cleaning shops get different value from each: Jobber (or a comparable field-service platform) for running client management, scheduling, invoicing, and payments across a whole business as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one job should cost from its footage and access before a business system is involved.
